source: Definitions written for this game in plain language, following NASA's own public explanations (NASA Glossary, NASA Systems Engineering Handbook SP-2016-6105 for margins and readiness levels, JPL Basics of Space Flight for trajectories and communications).
units: Each term has an id, the term as shown, a one- or two-sentence definition, and where in the game it matters (where_used).

terms.definition: The total change in speed a spacecraft can make with its engines, in metres per second. Every manoeuvre costs some: braking into orbit, landing, correcting the course. It is the currency of spaceflight.

The rule that links delta-v to propellant: each extra metre per second needs more propellant, and that propellant needs propellant to push it. The cost grows exponentially, which is why a little extra mass on the vehicle becomes a lot on the launch pad.
How efficiently an engine uses propellant, in seconds. A higher number means more delta-v from every kilogram of propellant.

How much energy the rocket must give the spacecraft beyond escaping Earth, in km²/s². The Moon needs slightly less than escape (a negative C3); Mars needs about 8 to 20. The higher it is, the less mass a rocket can send.
A chart of launch energy for every pair of launch and arrival dates. Its bright islands are the launch windows, and they look like pork chops.
The dates on which a mission can launch and still reach its target. For Mars it opens for a few weeks every 26 months, when the two planets line up.
The coasting path between two worlds. Given a launch date and an arrival date there is one arc that connects them, and it fixes how fast you must leave and how fast you arrive.
The braking burn that lets a destination's gravity capture the spacecraft. Miss it and the spacecraft flies past.

Getting from the top of an atmosphere to the ground: a heat shield takes the speed off, a parachute slows the fall, and engines land the last part. On Mars it takes about seven minutes and runs without help from Earth.
The spare capacity between what a design needs and what it has. Designs always grow as they are built, so NASA keeps 20 to 30 % of mass and power spare at the start.
NASA's nine-step scale of how proven a piece of hardware is, from an idea on paper (1) to flown in space (9). Low levels promise more and risk arriving late.
Carrying a second unit that takes over if the first fails. It costs mass and money and cuts the chance of losing that system about tenfold.
A power source that turns the heat of decaying plutonium into electricity, day and night, for decades. Low power, high cost, and its waste heat keeps the vehicle warm.
The share of a battery's capacity that can be used without wearing it out, typically about 80 %.
Switching nearly everything off to wait out darkness, keeping only heaters and a clock alive on the battery.
A crater floor near a lunar pole that sunlight never reaches. At about minus 230 °C it can hold water ice for billions of years.
The skyline as seen from a landing site. At the lunar poles the Sun and Earth skim it, so a ridge a few degrees high decides whether there is light and a radio link.
Talking straight to antennas on Earth with no relay. It only works while Earth is above the horizon, and it weakens with the square of the distance.
A satellite that receives data from the surface at short range and passes it to Earth with its own large antenna. Nearly all data from Mars rovers comes home this way.
NASA's three sites of giant antennas in California, Spain and Australia. Every deep-space mission shares them, so each gets only some hours a day.
How long a radio signal takes to cross the distance: 1.3 seconds to the Moon, 4 to 22 minutes to Mars. Beyond the Moon nobody can steer a vehicle live.
What a spacecraft does when something goes wrong: stop work, point at the Sun, call home and wait for instructions. Safe, and it costs days.
A day on Mars: 24 hours and 39 minutes.
The weeks when the Sun sits between Earth and Mars and drowns the radio link. Missions stop sending commands until it passes.
Landing by matching camera pictures of the ground to a map carried on board, so the lander knows where it is and can steer to a safe spot.
The round before launch in which each team answers for its own system. One No-Go stops the count.
Flying the same design hundreds of times against different luck to see how often it works. It shows the risk a single flight hides.
The number that fixes a flight's luck: the same design with the same seed always gives the same mission, which is what makes scores comparable.
